questions.question: What is the difference between Promise.all, allSettled, race, and any?
questions.title: Promises Combinators
questions.direct_answer: All four run an array of promises in parallel and return a single promise. Promise.all: fulfills with all values in order, or rejects on the FIRST failure (fail-fast, results lost). allSettled: always fulfills with [{status, value|reason}] — you handle each outcome yourself. race: settles the way the FIRST-settling promise settles (fulfilled or rejected). any: fulfills with the first FULFILLED value; rejects only if ALL reject.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: All four run an array of promises in parallel and return a single promise. Promise.all: fulfills with all values in order, or rejects on the FIRST failure (fail-fast, results lost). allSettled: always fulfills with [{status, value|reason}] — you handle each outcome yourself. race: settles the way the FIRST-settling promise settles (fulfilled or rejected). any: fulfills with the first FULFILLED value; rejects only if ALL reject.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph all
        A1[all inputs] -->|any rejects| AF[REJECT first error]
        A1 -->|all fulfill| AO[values array in order]
    end
    subgraph allSettled
        S1[all inputs] --> SO[outcome array - never rejects]
    end
    subgraph race
        R1[all inputs] --> RF[first SETTLEMENT wins]
    end
    subgraph any
        N1[all inputs] -->|first fulfill| NO[value]
        N1 -->|all reject| NA[AggregateError]
    end
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The fail-fast asymmetry (the design reasoning to articulate): all is for AND-logic — the composed operation is only valid if every part succeeds, so one failure invalidates the whole batch. allSettled is for OR-at-the-batch-level — the operation survives partial loss. This maps to backend semantics: all composes like a database transaction (all-or-nothing), allSettled like a bulk operation with per-item error reporting.

Implementing race/any from scratch (the classic follow-up exercise): race is a new promise whose resolve/reject are wired to every input's then/catch — the first one to fire wins and the rest become no-ops (because the settled promise ignores further settlement). any wraps each rejection into a counter — only when the rejection count equals the input length does the outer promise reject with an AggregateError collecting the reasons.

The cancellation gap (the honest limitation): none of the combinators cancel losers. After race picks a winner, the losing fetches continue consuming bandwidth; after all fails fast, in-flight requests still complete server-side. Cancellation requires AbortController plumbing (pass one signal to every fetch, call abort when you're done waiting) — the pattern production code uses: `const ctrl = new AbortController(); const reqs = urls.map(u => fetch(u, {signal: ctrl.signal})); try { await Promise.all(reqs) } catch { ctrl.abort() }`.
